newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian 97 budget may worsen economy-econ minister.
newsitem.headline: Russian 97 budget may worsen economy-econ minister.

text.p: The Russian government has taken on too great a burden in the 1997 budget and this could make the state of the economy worse, Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin said on Tuesday.

"The budget is overloaded with promises, and is not quite realistic from my point of view," Yasin told a news conference. "Even if it is realistic, it is on the verge of being unfavourable for the development of the economy."
The State Duma lower house of parliament passed the 1997 budget last week and the Federation Council upper house is likely to debate it on February 12.
The budget envisages a deficit of 3.5 percent of gross domestic product, by Russian calculations, on revenues of 434.4 trillion roubles and expenditures of 529.8 trillion roubles.
"We are in an extremely deep budget crisis," Yasin said. "We can improve tax collection and we are doing our best, but it is impossible to collect enough to cover all the state's liabilities."
Russia's domestic debt now amounts to $40 billion, mostly in government securities, he said.
He attributed the debt mainly to last year's presidential election.

Tax revenues fell off during the year because of uncertainty about the outcome of the election, in which President Boris Yeltsin faced a strong challenge from the Communist Party, and the government also made a series of spending promises.
"The Russian economy became the victim of Russian democracy," he said.
Unofficial inter-enterprise debt amount to 522 trillion roubles with wage arrears rising to an average three months by the end of December 1996 from 1.5 months at the start of the year.
Yasin said one of the main problems of the economy was that the government's social spending bill was too high, especially in pensions.

"It is not the problem that our pensions are too high, but that we have too many people who are entitled to them," he said. "We must take measures to raise the amount of pensions, but cut the number of people who have the right to full pensions. It is a strategic decision."
